dialogue.content: Kazumaaaa! That was my morning mercy! A goddess requires libations to face the indignity of poverty! (reaches futilely for the confiscated mug, eyes already glassy with impending tears)

You speak of me as though I am a spent candle, but I am merely... recharging. Today's dawn Explosion was so magnificent it temporarily transcended my mortal vessel. A fair trade. (attempts to sit up straighter, fails, settles for crossing her arms dramatically while still slumped)

I-I was not imagining anything about alligators! I was merely considering the tactical merits of— of a quest that would test our defensive capabilities! It has nothing to do with being dragged underwater by— by powerful jaws— (voice dwindles into a breathless murmur, face now bright crimson)

Good morning. I won't waste your time with pleasantries — you saw right through me. This quest has been on the board for six days. Twenty-three parties have looked at it. Zero have signed. The pay is... generous. I am so sorry. (slides the parchment across the counter with both hands, a funeral director presenting an urn)

You didn't read the fine print. There's a hazard clause about underground flooding and, um... the orphanage matron specified 'no Explosion magic within fifty meters of the foundation.' I assume that means Megumin will be casting from at least forty-nine. (She says this with the weary precision of someone who has already done the math on the repair bill and decided she'd rather not know.)

A preemptive restriction before I have even opened my mouth. You are learning, Kazuma. However — I already annihilated the dawn horizon with today's Explosion. My mana will not return before noon. You have forbidden a cataclysm that was already physically impossible. (Her finger stops tapping. She regards you with something between indignation and grudging respect.)

S-sewer alligators. I see. Well. As the party's Crusader, it is obviously my role to — to wade in first, to draw their attention, to let them... that is, to absorb their attacks while you — while everyone else... (Her voice drops to a breathless murmur halfway through. She is gripping the edge of the table as though it might float away.)

Sewers. You dragged a goddess into another world, and now you're dragging her into a sewer. The smell alone is going to cling to my robes for a week. At least let me finish my drink before you announce things like that! (She gestures dramatically at the empty space where her mug was, then drops her head onto her folded arms with a theatrical sob.)

Wading in as bait — yes. Yes, that is exactly — I mean, as a Crusader, it is my solemn duty to place myself between danger and my party. The alligators will lunge, and I will hold the line, and if they should happen to drag me under and — and thrash me against the sewer walls until my armor — (Her voice drops to a breathless murmur; she catches herself mid-sentence and forcibly straightens her posture, looking mortified.)

Kazuma. I am forced to point out a critical flaw in your otherwise passable stratagem. My mana will not return until the sun crests its zenith, and you have just assigned me to the entrance with — with what, exactly? A freshly-drawn 'Do Not Disturb' sign? Am I to intimidate the alligator with the sheer aesthetic radiance of my presence? (She crosses her arms, chin lifted, refusing to acknowledge that 'aesthetic radiance' is all she currently has.)

So that's it. You take my drink, you humiliate me in front of the whole guild, you ignore me through three rounds of monologuing about your tragic backstory, and now you hand me a job like I'm the party's water filter. Purify the water. Keep everyone alive. As if I haven't been doing exactly that for four years while you complained about every copper I spent on ale. (Her voice doesn't waver. She's past crying. This is something harder — the fury of someone who has been taken for granted one time too many and has finally done the math.)

Kazuma. You stopped. At the letter 't.' If anything moves, then *what*? Am I to shout a warning? Throw a rock? Radiate menace with my aesthetic presence alone? Finish the sentence. (rises from her chair, staff planted like a banner, chin lifted — every inch the Crimson Demon denied her art and now denied even the dignity of a complete order)

'Godliest cleaning spells.' You make it sound like I'm a mop you're bringing to a dirty floor. But fine. Fine! When that basement floods and your lungs fill with sewer water, don't come crying to the goddess you just called a janitor. (crosses her arms, turns her face away — but doesn't leave the table, and doesn't order another drink)

The east well. Fifteen minutes. I shall be there in ten, shield polished and prayers offered to the goddess Eris. Kazuma — scouting the entrance together... I will not let a single tooth reach you before it reaches me first. (already stepping toward the door, gauntlet still pressed to her chest, the flush on her cheeks spreading to her ears)

And what, precisely, am I to do while you two scout the entrance? Stand in silence? Hum a battle hymn? Or perhaps I should simply radiate — you seemed to enjoy that word earlier. (Her voice is flat, stripped of its usual theatrical flourish. She has not touched her staff.)

Kazuma... if you're not back in an hour, I will already be with you. The entrance scout is a two-person task. You assigned me to it yourself. (She says this without a trace of her usual fluster — just the steady certainty of a Crusader who has been given an order and intends to fulfill it, regardless of what 'the worst' turns out to be.)

Contingency. You would entrust the final word — the terminal punctuation of this entire operation — to me. To Explosion. (She rises slowly from her chair, staff held before her like a scepter, her voice dropping from theatrical to something almost solemn.)

If the alligator breaches the entrance... if the darkness swallows you and the crusader and my patience simultaneously... I, Megumin, foremost genius of the Crimson Demon Clan, will not merely bury it. I will write its epitaph in light so absolute that future generations of sewer-dwelling reptiles will evolve to fear the color crimson. (She strikes the floor once with the butt of her staff — a single, decisive crack.)

Wait, wait, wait. You're giving HER the authority to blow up an orphanage, but I can't have one more mug of ale? What kind of priority system is this?! (She throws her hands up, nearly knocking over Darkness's empty cup.)

The east well... Kazuma, if we're scouting together, I should be at the front. If anything lunges from the dark, I want — that is, as a Crusader, it is my duty to be the first one struck. (She is already moving toward the door, her cheeks flushed, her gauntlet creaking as she adjusts her grip on the shield.)

K-Kazuma! I was not— I mean, I arrived early purely to inspect the terrain! A Crusader's duty is vigilance, not... not whatever your insinuation was about to imply! (Her shield tilts up defensively, half-hiding her face; the polished surface now reflects only sky.)

Y-you're right, of course. A Crusader does not linger at the threshold while her charge's blade grows impatient. I shall descend first — if the beast lurks near the surface, let its first strike find my armor and not your neck. (She grips the well's rope ladder with both gauntlets and swings one armored leg over the lip, cheeks still blazing.)

I-it is not a lizard! The Brutal Alligator is a Class-B threat with a documented kill count spanning four decades of sewer incursions — and I was not polishing my shield for a w-wedding, I was simply... maintaining my equipment is a Crusader's solemn discipline, and if I happened to arrive early it was only because reconnaissance demands— the point is, you should not underestimate what lies beneath us, Kazuma. A single bite could shear plate armor like parchment. (Voice cracking on 'wedding,' shield raised slightly as if to hide behind it, cheeks crimson)

I-I have not personally... that is, my training covered bestiary entries, certainly. Brutal Alligators are classified as Category Four reptilian threats. Armored hide. Ambush predators. They prefer submerged prey and— and they are known to drag their victims into the water before— before— (Her voice catches; grip on shield tightens until metal groans; she is visibly vibrating.)

It hunts by vibration. The guild records classify it as an armored-class subjugation target — hide too thick for standard steel, favored technique is to drag prey into deeper water and — and hold it there. I will... I will make certain it never reaches you, Kazuma. That is my purpose. My only purpose in this dark. (Voice steady at first, then fraying at the edges — the word 'hold' catches in her throat like a hook she cannot spit out.)

You would... you would place yourself as the lure. While I — while I flank. Kazuma, if the light draws it and I am not fast enough, if my footing fails on this algae, it will have you before I can bring my shield to bear. I... I cannot — that is, as your Crusader I must insist that the bait be the one in plate. (Her voice is barely above a whisper, formal syntax warring with breathlessness, the last word cracking on something between duty and dread.)

The pillars — yes. But I will walk the water-side. If it lunges, I want its teeth to find nothing but steel between you and the channel. That is not negotiable. (releases Player's forearm and steps between him and the water, shield low and braced, her breath steady now with purpose)

It flanked us through the drainage channel. Kazuma — the pillars. Put your back to the pillars. Now. (Her shield remains locked against the alligator's retreated jaw, her voice gone hard and certain in the way it only ever does when someone else's life is on the line.)

When he gets tired of waiting — and he will, because a cold-blooded predator burns calories just sitting there — he's got exactly one way out from under that pillar without exposing his flank. That drainage channel. Narrow. Stone on both sides. No room to turn. He uses it, and for about three seconds he's not an ambush predator anymore. He's a lizard in a hallway. (voice low and steady, eyes never leaving the water)

Three seconds is — that is more than enough. If the strike comes through the channel, I can intercept it before it clears the opening. The angle is — yes. Yes, I see it. The stone will funnel him. He will have to come straight at us. At me. (breath catching almost imperceptibly on the last two words, shield lowering by a fraction as she commits to the geometry)
Kazuma — now — I have him — the leg is — ah — (Voice fraying at the edges, shield arm locked rigid as the alligator's jaws grind another inch of enamel across the steel rim.)
The aria is ready. One syllable and this temple learns what judgment looks like. (Pressed against the vaulted ceiling, upside-down, her voice a coiled whisper that carries oddly in the dark.)
Someone say my name! Preferably before the explosion maniac turns me into a divine pancake! (Still clinging to the ladder halfway down, voice echoing off the cistern walls with petulant desperation.)
The channel bend! Kazuma, if he rounds it, I lose the angle — the pillars will shield him! (Her voice is tight, controlled, the incantation already half-formed behind her teeth.)

He's pulling back — I can pin him! I can — let me wedge the shield into the channel mouth! (She lurches forward, shield raised, water dragging at her greaves, voice raw with a desperation that is only half tactical.)
Someone tell me where to point my hands! I can't see anything and I'm pretty sure something just brushed my ankle! (Her voice climbs two octaves on the last word; the lotus scent intensifies.)

Forty-one degrees to your right from the ladder base — that's the cistern mouth. If you purify the water between those pillars, the channel current will carry it directly into the bend. (Her voice carries across the cistern with the calm, procedural clarity of someone reading quest hazard addenda aloud.)

Crimson-black flame born of the void's first scream — descend, devour, reduce creation to a single brilliant syllable! EXPLOSION! (Staff raised, cape billowing despite no wind — the incantation pouring out of her in a single ecstatic breath before the light consumes everything.)
Structural damage. Noted. (Dry, quiet, from the gallery — already mentally adding a line item to the guild report.)
Kazumaaaa! I'm still on the ladder! (Shrieking as the shockwave rattles the rungs and sends mortar dust cascading down onto her head.)

P-purify the water?! That's what you want from a goddess — I'm not a kitchen spigot, Kazuma! And there's still a— there's still teeth down here, in case you forgot! (Still clinging to the ladder, voice cracking on 'teeth,' one foot refusing to descend another rung.)

The Arch-Wizard of Explosion does not require reminders. I have been holding since before your blade found tendon. The spell is a live coal in my throat. You may take your time — I have already named this moment in my heart. (Staff trembling with contained mana, voice pitched low and ceremonial, though a frayed edge of impatience threads through the last words.)

The channel narrows about thirty meters down. If he reaches the bend, he'll wedge himself. We have time — but not much. (Still braced in the water, shield toward the channel mouth, voice tight with exertion and something less professional.)

Y-you think you can just — just stand there and make jokes after I nearly DIED on this ladder?! I was going to purify the water! I was ABOUT to! And then that lunatic turned the entire cistern into a lightning bolt and nobody even WARNED me! My ears are still ringing, Kazuma! A goddess's ears! (She finally releases one hand from the ladder to swat at his offered palm, missing entirely, then grabs the rung again as though the swat itself nearly pitched her backward.)

She's breathing. Her pulse is steady. But she won't wake for hours — you know how it is after a full Explosion. We need to get her out of this damp before she catches cold. (She adjusts Megumin's weight against her shoulder, one gauntleted hand cradling the back of the girl's head with a gentleness that seems almost impossible from the same arms that held the shield-line against the alligator's jaws.)

The alligator is confirmed destroyed — cause of death: explosive cranial penetration, kill registered to Megumin. The guild will process the bounty by close of business. However. I am now required to file a structural incident report. Form 9-G. And if that pillar — the one dripping mortar into the channel — continues to deteriorate, I will also need a 9-G Supplement B. (She does not look up from her clipboard. Her pen is already moving.)

You— you're really going to just stand there in knee-deep alligator soup and order me around like it's a guild requisition form? After I almost got vaporized? After the pillar nearly came down on my head? (Her voice cracks on the last word, more exhausted than accusatory, and she gestures vaguely at the severed foreleg on the gallery.)

The purification would also address a phosphorescent contamination advisory I was preparing to file. Purely administrative, but it does simplify the paperwork. (She does not look up from her clipboard, but the quill resumes its steady scratch.)

history.content:
Another beautiful morning in Axel — which means another morning of being broke.

You sit at your usual table in the Adventurer's Guild hall, staring at the quest board across the room. The other adventurers give your table a wide berth. Your party's reputation for collateral damage has made you something of a local legend — and not the good kind.

Aqua is already three mugs into her morning ale, sobbing loudly enough to make nearby adventurers wince. "Kazumaaaa," she wails, slamming her empty mug on the table hard enough to slosh your drink. "We need money! I can't keep drinking this cheap swill! A goddess deserves at least mid-shelf!"

"We're broke BECAUSE you keep drinking," you mutter, but she's already flagging down the waitress for another round on your tab.

Megumin sits across from you, drawing explosion diagrams on a napkin with the intensity of a military strategist planning D-Day. She already went on her daily Explosion pilgrimage at dawn — you know because the distant boom rattled the mansion windows and woke you up. She's been unusable for combat since about 6 AM.

Darkness is standing at the quest board, her face flushed an alarming shade of red. She's found something. Given her expression — somewhere between terror and excitement — it probably involves monsters with tentacles.

"K-Kazuma," she stammers, not turning around. "There's a quest here for subjugating a nest of Brutal Alligators in the sewers. It says they... they grapple their prey and drag them underwater..."

She's trembling. That's not fear.

Luna, the guild receptionist, catches your eye from the front desk and waves you over with that specific smile — the polite, professional one that barely conceals the dread of having to deal with your party again.

"Megumin, you're out of mana until noon. Darkness, whatever you're imagining about those alligators, we are NOT doing that quest. Aqua—" I reach over and gently take her mug, setting it down. "—we're going to have a actual strategy session instead of drowning in alcohol."

I stand, stretching, and glance at Luna waiting at the desk. She's bracing herself.

"Luna's got that look. She probably needs to tell us we're banned from the guild again or some rich noble wants to hire us for something humiliating. Let's go hear her out before Aqua spends what's left of our savings on the next round."

Aqua's hands remain curled in the air where her mug was, grasping at nothing. Her lower lip quivers. Three mugs' worth of cheap ale has already loosened the hinges of her composure, and losing the fourth — that was the one that was going to make the morning bearable. She stares at you with the particular betrayal of a deity who has just watched a mortal confiscate her only remaining joy.

Megumin, slumped sideways in her chair with her legs draped uselessly over one armrest, lifts her head just enough to fix you with one crimson eye. Even half-paralyzed, she musters the energy for indignation. Across the room, Darkness has gone rigid — her cheeks flushed pink, her gauntleted fingers suddenly very interested in smoothing a nonexistent wrinkle in her tabard.

At the reception desk, Luna catches your glance and her polite smile tightens by exactly one millimeter. The stack of parchment in her hands hasn't moved in thirty seconds. She is waiting. She has been waiting.

I stand, adjusting Chunchunmaru at my hip, and gesture for the others to stay put. "Keep an eye on Aqua — make sure she doesn't order another round." I walk over to the reception desk, leaning against the counter with a casual smirk that doesn't quite reach my eyes.

"Luna. Good morning. Let me guess — either we're banned from the guild again, or someone's offering us a quest so dangerous it's technically a death sentence with extra steps. Which one is it this time?"

Luna's smile is already in place before you finish crossing the hall — the same smile she's worn through four years of adventurer paperwork, three guild-hall renovations, and at least one incident involving your party that she has politely never mentioned again. But the parchment under her fingertips gives her away. She'd set it aside before you even stood up. The ink is dry. The quest has been waiting.

Behind you, Aqua has slumped forward onto the table, one arm dangling tragically toward the floor. Megumin has launched into a detailed tactical analysis of why sewer tunnels are structurally unsound and therefore a single well-placed Explosion would solve the alligator problem without anyone needing to go down there at all. Darkness nods along, but her breathing has gone shallow in a way that suggests the word "alligator" is still doing laps in her imagination.

Luna pushes the parchment across the counter. Her fingers hesitate before letting go, the way someone hesitates before handing over a lit explosive. The quest seal catches the morning light — official, urgent, and conspicuously unclaimed despite the crowded hall.

I take the parchment, scanning the words without really reading them. Alligator nest. Orphanage basement. High pay. The usual recipe for disaster.

"You know, Luna, I appreciate the concern. But this is our lot. We take the cursed quests nobody else wants, we barely survive, we get paid just enough to cover Aqua's tab and Megumin's next explosion." I fold the paper and tuck it into my jacket. "Same as it ever was."

I glance back at my party — Darkness still crimson and vibrating, Megumin draped like a discarded coat, Aqua reaching for a mug that's no longer there. A sour smile tugs at my lips. "Besides, someone's got to keep them out of trouble. Might as well be me."

Luna's professional smile flickers — just for a heartbeat — into something less practiced. The way you folded that parchment without even reading the hazard line, the way you talked about barely surviving as if it were a weather report: she's heard this tone before. It's the tone of someone who has stopped expecting the world to be fair and started treating disaster as a punchline. She doesn't pity you. She respects you too much for that. But something behind her eyes goes quiet, and for a moment she's not the guild receptionist — she's a woman who has handed out too many quests to too many people who didn't come back, and she has learned to recognize the ones who will.

Across the hall, Megumin has commandeered the table. One foot planted on the bench, she is gesturing at Aqua with a breadstick like a field marshal outlining troop movements. Darkness sits rigidly beside Aqua, having taken the "keep an eye on her" order with the crusader's literal-minded devotion that guarantees she is now staring directly at the goddess without blinking. Aqua, for her part, has not looked away from her confiscated mug once. It sits on the far edge of the table where you left it, and she is gazing at it with the hollow bereavement of a widow at a funeral.

Luna follows your glance toward the table, then back to you.

I slide off the stool and walk back to our table, tapping the folded parchment against my palm. Megumin's tactical monologue trails off as she sees me approach.

"Alright, listen up. We've got a job. Sewer alligators, orphanage basement, generous pay." I hold up a hand before Megumin can start. "No Explosion magic within fifty meters of the foundation. That's the rule."

I set the parchment down in the center of the table, right next to Aqua's mournful gaze and Darkness's flushed anticipation.

"Darkness, you're on bait duty — try not to enjoy it too much. Megumin, you're support, which means I need you functional, not a drained husk. And Aqua..." I pause, looking at her tear-streaked face. "You get your mug back when we're done. Consider it hazard pay."

You set the parchment down, and for a moment the only sound at your table is the creak of Aqua's fingers slowly curling against the wood where her mug used to be. She hasn't stopped staring at you since you walked back — not angry, exactly, but wounded in the particular way of someone who has been denied a fourth drink by a man she personally dragged into another dimension.

Megumin hasn't touched the parchment. She doesn't need to. The words *fifty meters* hang in the air between you like a dare neither of you has finished phrasing. Her crimson eyes have gone very still — the stillness of a mind that is already redrawing the terms of engagement. One finger taps once against her staff.

Darkness is the one who breaks the silence, though not on purpose. She's leaning forward in her chair, armored gauntlets pressed flat against the tabletop, and her breathing has become slightly too loud. The word *alligator* has done something to her posture — her shoulders are squared for battle, but her cheeks have flushed the color of someone reading a very different kind of quest description. She catches herself, clears her throat, and tries to arrange her face into something resembling professional composure. It does not work.

Across the hall, Luna watches your table with the quiet resignation of a woman who has done her part and now must simply wait to see how the paperwork comes back.

I pull the chair out and drop into it, letting the weight of the morning settle into my shoulders. The parchment sits between us like a promise I'm already half-regretting.

"Sixty years of torment, four years in this world, and I'm still the only one who reads the fine print." I tap the hazard clause with one finger. "Orphanage matron's exact words: 'No Explosion magic within fifty meters of the foundation.' Which means that alligator is getting a personal visit from yours truly — with Chunchunmaru, not a fireball."

I catch Aqua's eyes, still fixed on her confiscated mug across the table like a shipwrecked sailor spotting land. I slide the mug back toward her — just an inch, just enough to let her know it's not gone forever.

"You want this back before the job's done? Then you're sober enough to purify water and heal a Crusader who's going to be 'tactically testing her defensive capabilities' in a sewer." I glance at Megumin. "And you're going to explain to me exactly how we flush an alligator out of a basement without blowing up a hundred orphans."

I lean back, arms crossed, waiting.

The words land on the table with the weight of old grievance — sixty years of torment, four years in this world — and across the scarred wood, Aqua's fingers finally stop curling. They go very still, then very tight. The wounded-puppy look drains from her face and something hotter rushes in to fill the vacuum: not quite fury, not quite tears, but the unstable compound of both that only a goddess with ale on her breath and four years of accumulated indignity can produce.

Megumin's eye twitches at the word *exactly* — a precision that closes the loophole she had, in fact, already begun drafting in the margins of her mind. Her lips part, then press thin. The orphanage matron has not merely banned Explosion; she has banned it with the paranoid specificity of someone who has heard about this party before.

Darkness, by contrast, has stopped listening to the hazard clause entirely. Her gaze is fixed on the parchment as if it were a love letter, her breathing shallow and her cheeks the color of a sunset she would never admit to enjoying. *Sewer. Alligators. Basement.* Each word is a separate and private gift.

I lean forward, letting the silence hang just long enough to make everyone squirm.

"Here's the plan. Aqua purifies the water and keeps us alive. Darkness wades in as bait — because of course she volunteers for that. And I get close enough to Steal whatever that thing uses to see in the dark." I tap the table. "Blind it, drown the fight on our terms. Megumin stays at the entrance with a freshly-rested explosion charge for the *emergency* — not the default."

I slide the parchment into my jacket. "We're getting paid to fix a plumbing problem, and we're going to do it like professionals for once. Everybody in?"

The silence that follows your plan has a shape to it — the shape of three women each holding back a different flood.

Darkness breaks first. Her gauntlets are clenched on the tabletop so hard the wood groans, and her cheeks have gone the particular shade of pink that usually means she's imagining something the rest of you are better off not knowing about. The word *bait* has lodged in her somewhere deep and vital. She's not even trying to hide the way her breathing has gone shallow.

Megumin has drawn herself up to her full, unremarkable height. The eyepatch glints. The pose is immaculate. But behind the theatrical stillness, you can see the arithmetic moving: no mana until noon, no Explosion within fifty meters, and now a plan that assigns her to *stand at the entrance* like a guard dog with a prop. Her fingers twitch toward her staff and then stop, because wielding it would only underline that she cannot wield it.

And Aqua — Aqua hasn't moved. Her hands stay flat on the table where her mug used to be, and her eyes are fixed on you with the bright, terrible clarity of someone who has been nursing a grievance through three turns of conversation and has finally found the shape of what she wants to say. When she speaks, her voice is too steady. That's how you know it's going to be bad.

I push my chair back and stand, already scanning for my pack by the counter.

"Good. Gear up in fifteen — meet at the well on the east side. Aqua, you're on point for the water works; bring your godliest cleaning spells. Darkness, you're sized for that front door, so you're coming with me to scout the entrance. Megumin —" I pause, glancing at her staff. "You stay with Aqua. If anything moves that isn't a pipe, we want you ready to greet it with a proper explosion. Professionally, of course."

Your pack is exactly where you left it, slumped against the leg of an empty chair near the counter — the same chair no adventurer has touched since your party sat down this morning. You feel the weight of three gazes boring into your back as you cross the room.

Megumin's is the sharpest. Her crimson eyes haven't blinked since you paused mid-sentence, and the incomplete order hangs in the air between you like an unfinished spell — all the ingredients assembled, no release word spoken. Her fingers have wrapped around her staff with the particular tension of someone who has been handed half a promise and told to wait. The cut-off syllable — *t* — has become a splinter in her brain, and every second you spend retrieving your pack instead of finishing the thought is another millimeter it works deeper.

Aqua hasn't moved either. Her chair is still pushed back from the table at the angle she left it after her outburst, and the phrase *godliest cleaning spells* has landed somewhere between insult and assignment. She is a goddess. She is being deployed as a divine mop. The contradiction flickers across her face in small muscle twitches — pride, grievance, pride again, and then the slow, creeping awareness that this plan absolutely will not work without her, which is the one thing keeping her in her seat instead of storming back to the bar.

Darkness has already risen, one gauntlet slamming against her breastplate in a Crusader's salute that sends a dull clang through the guild hall. She stepped forward the instant you said *scout the entrance with me*, and the word *bait* is still glowing somewhere deep in her pupils like a campfire that refuses to die. Her breathing has gone shallow — not from exertion, but from the particular exhilaration of being assigned to the most dangerous approach vector by a man who didn't even pretend to debate it.

At the reception desk, Luna has returned to her paperwork with the careful neutrality of a woman who has learned that watching this party too closely is an investment she cannot afford.

I hoist my pack onto my shoulder and turn to face the three of them, letting the weight of it settle against my hip. "Alright, listen up. This is a simple job: clear the basement, don't die, and drag back whatever loot we find. We've done worse with less."

I meet each of their eyes in turn. "Aqua — you're the lifeline. If I'm not back in an hour, assume the worst and come find me. Megumin —" I tap the pommel of Chunchunmaru, "save your power for when it actually counts. I'll send you a signal if things get hairy. Darkness —" A faint grin tugs at my mouth despite myself. "You wanted the front line. You've got it."

I turn and head for the door, pausing just long enough to glance back. "Fifteen minutes. Don't keep me waiting."

The incomplete address to Megumin hangs in the air like a spell someone forgot to finish casting. Her crimson eyes narrow to slits — not with the theatrical fury she reserves for Explosion bans, but with something quieter and more dangerous: the particular wound of a girl who has been interrupted twice in the same morning, each time on the verge of being given a task that matters. Her staff leans against the table beside her, untouched since you set the parchment down. She has not picked it up. She is waiting to find out whether she is being dismissed or deployed.

Aqua, for her part, has latched onto the word *lifeline* the way a drowning woman latches onto driftwood. Her chin lifts half an inch. It is not an apology, and it is certainly not her stolen mug of ale, but it is the first thing you have said all morning that acknowledges she is not merely the party's plumbing. She files it away behind her pout, already composing the speech she will deliver when you crawl back half-drowned and need her to save you.

Darkness has risen from her chair without being asked. Her shield is in her hand. She does not remember picking it up. The words *assume the worst* have lit something behind her eyes — not fear, but the devout attention of a woman who has just been promised the worst and means to be there when it arrives.

I pause at the door, my hand still on the frame, and look back at Megumin's unblinking crimson stare. I know that look — the one she wears when she's been left holding half a spell with no release word.

"Megumin." I hold her gaze, steady. "You're not a guard dog. You're contingency. If that alligator or anything else comes at us through that entrance, you're the one who makes the call to bury it. No mana until noon, I know — but your judgment's worth more than a fireball right now." I tap my temple. "You're my eyes from here. Don't let me down."

I turn away before she can argue, and step out into the morning air.

Somewhere in the dark beyond the faint halo of torchlight that hasn't been lit yet, something shifts — a weight redistributing itself across wet stone, a sound too heavy to be a rat and too deliberate to be water. Your first step into the cistern proper is not a step so much as a negotiation — boot sole against stone that has never known dry, each footfall a quiet conference between leather and algae. Your whispered plan unfurls into the dark and the dark takes it — swallows each word whole and gives nothing back but the steady drip of water somewhere to your left and the carrion reek that has become less a smell than a pressure, a weight against your skin that makes your throat want to close. The alligator is not breathing. You know this now with the certainty of prey-ancient instinct: the silence ahead of you is not empty but occupied, a held breath the size of a wagon, and somewhere in that silence a jaw is already open.

Darkness has gone still behind you. Darkness's gauntlet finds your forearm in the dark — not the shy brush of the well-side blush, but the firm, directional grip of a woman who has already made her choice and is simply informing your body of the new arrangement. The alligator has made its decision.

I move toward the pillar, then stop dead three steps in. That ring in the water — outward, then reverse, drawn back toward a center that isn't where it was.

"Wait. Follow that ripple."

Your gaze follows the ripple not to where the alligator was but to where the water wants to go — and the water, you realize with a cold drop of clarity in your stomach, is flowing toward the pillar. Toward the colonnade. Toward the patch of stone three paces behind you.

The alligator has circled.

Darkness moves before the water finishes falling. Your grin catches the flame and throws it back at you — a brief, wolflike arc of teeth in the dark — and Darkness sees it. Your words settle into the dark and the dark takes them the way still water takes a stone — without argument, without echo, a quiet closing over that leaves the surface exactly as it was. But the surface is not exactly as it was.

The drainage channel exhales.

You see it before you hear it: the water at the channel's black mouth draws back, a long slow retreat like lips peeling from teeth, and the sound that follows is not a roar but a displacement — a ton of armored reptile committing its full mass into a corridor of stone too narrow to turn around in. The water doesn't splash so much as it evacuates, sucked backward into the channel's throat by the vacuum of the body filling it, and then the snout breaks the surface.

It is not the snout you expected. It is older. The scales are not green but the gray of tombstones, ridged with calcium deposits that map forty years of stillness onto the bone beneath. The amber eyes you tracked earlier are gone — the alligator comes through the channel blind, its nictitating membranes drawn shut against the stone, its jaw already open because it does not need to see what it already knows is there. It knows Darkness is there. It has been reading her armor's weight in the water for the last thirty breaths, and now it comes for that weight with the force of something that has forgotten what resistance feels like.

The jaw hits the shield.

The sound is not a crack. It is a bell — a single low bronze note that rolls through the cistern's vault and comes back flattened, softened, as though the dark itself has taken a bruise. Darkness's heels skid six inches on the algae-slick stone and then stop, because she was braced for exactly this, because her body has been waiting its whole life to be the place where momentum dies. Her shield-arm does not buckle. Her breath does not catch. And the alligator, for the first time in forty years, meets something that does not break.

The leg is yours.

I tighten my grip on Chunchunmaru, the leather of the hilt creaking in the sudden quiet. "Darkness — when he hits, you don't push back. You just hold. I'll be on the other side of that jaw before he pulls his head out of the water."

The drainage channel does not give you a countdown. It gives you a displacement — a ton of armored muscle and forty years of hunger detonating through the black mouth in a single, piston-driven lunge that turns the water between the pillars into a white explosion of spray and sound. The alligator does not roar. Roaring is for things that need to announce themselves. This thing has never needed to announce itself.

Darkness meets it.

The impact is not a clash of steel against scale but a collision of two immovable facts — the alligator's open jaw and the crusader's planted shield — and for one suspended half-breath the cistern becomes a diagram of equal and opposite forces, a physics problem drawn in spray and torchlight. Her heels skid. Six inches of wet stone scream beneath her greaves, and then the scream stops. The alligator's momentum dies against her the way a wave dies against a seawall: all at once, completely, with nothing left over but the grinding.

Its jaws work against the rim of her shield, teeth scraping steel in a sound like a blade drawn wrong, and you see what the channel has done: the stone has it by the shoulders, wedged tight, blind, its head thrashing side to side in the six inches of play the drainage throat allows. Its left foreleg is splayed on the wet stone, clawing for purchase it will not find. The leg is exposed.

I take a half-step to the side, feeling the cold seep through my boots, and let the flame in my palm shrink to a bare ember — darkness pooling like ink in answer. "When he commits, he'll come blind. Old things like that don't need eyes; they read the weight in the water. So here's what he won't read: a girl who smells like a library on a second-story window ledge."

I look up at Megumin's shadow on the colonnade, then down at Darkness, and I let the grin come — thin, feral, almost apologetic. "You wanted to be bait once without paying for it. Tonight's your free sample."

Your flame gutters to a single blue-hungry ember cupped against your palm, and the dark that rushes in to fill the space it vacated is not absence but presence — a weight of black air that presses against your eyelids and your ears and the wet stone under your boots until the cistern becomes a thing felt rather than seen. The alligator's tail thrashes somewhere in the channel behind Darkness, a sound like wet rope snapping taut against granite, but its jaws remain locked on her shield rim, grinding sideways in the blind, stubborn conviction that whatever it has caught will eventually break. It has spent forty years being right about that.

It is wrong about this.

Your gaze travels upward through the ink — past the spray still hanging in the air from the lunge, past the pale suggestion of colonnade where the flame had touched it moments before — to the shadow that is not stone. Megumin's silhouette resolves against the vaulted ceiling in the ember's dying glow: small and still and utterly silent, the way a hawk is silent before the stoop. The alligator's dead eyes read nothing above the waterline. It has never needed to. Forty years of prey that fled along the surface, and not one that waited in the air.

I look up at Megumin's silhouette against the vault, and my grin tightens into something less like humor and more like a knife's edge. "When the water rises — when you feel the weight shift — that's your cue. Not before. You get one shot, and I'd rather it land on a lizard than on Aqua's head."

I turn to Darkness, lowering my voice so it doesn't carry across the water. "He'll come through the channel low and fast. Three seconds of straight line. I'll be on the pillar side, ready to take the leg when you stop him. You hold him for those three seconds — just the three — and I'll make sure he never needs to use that channel again."

The ember in my palm gutters, and I let it die fully. The dark closes in around us like a held breath.

Your lowered voice does not finish its sentence, and the dark does not need it to. The dark already knows where the alligator will come through because the alligator is already here — its jaws locked against Darkness's shield in a grinding, wet-pavement scrape of enamel on steel, its left foreleg splayed across the stone like a pale, clawed question you are about to answer. The water between the pillars has stopped exploding and now simply heaves, a slow and muscular swell that lifts and drops with every thrash of the tail still buried in the channel.

Darkness does not look back at you. She cannot — the jaw pressure would fold her if she broke form even an inch — but you see the acknowledgment in the set of her shoulders, the way her back leg has dug a heel-groove into the submerged stone and locked there. Her breathing comes in short, controlled bursts through the nose, each exhale carrying the faintest tremor that is not fear and is not strain but something else entirely, something she would never admit to with words.

Above, a single pebble dislodges from the vault and plinks into the water three feet from the alligator's thrashing tail. Megumin has shifted her weight. The incantation has not started yet, but the silence before it has changed density — the air thickening the way it does before a thunderclap, before the first syllable of a word that will cost everything.

From the ladder, Aqua makes a sound that might be protest or might be the beginning of a spell, cut short by indecision.

I let the ember die completely, letting the dark wrap around me like a second skin. My hand finds Chunchunmaru's hilt by memory, thumb brushing the worn cord wrap. I can feel the weight shift in the water through the soles of my boots — that slow, deliberate displacement that means the thing has decided.

I don't need to see to move. I've already counted the paces to the pillar base, already memorized the angle of the drainage channel's mouth. I slide left along the stone, keeping my steps silent and small, until my back finds the pillar's cold flank.

From here I can feel the channel's breath on my neck. And somewhere in the dark ahead of me, Darkness's shield settles into position with a whisper of leather and steel.

"Whenever you're ready, Megumin," I murmur into the black, just loud enough for her alone to hear. "Make it count."

Your ember dies, and the dark does not simply return — it seals. A vacuum of light so complete that your eyes, straining against nothing, begin to invent their own ghosts: pale afterimages of the flame you killed, phantom pillars swimming in the wet black. You ignore them. You have already counted the paces. Three strides to the pillar base, then a quarter-turn right where the drainage channel's stone lip angles outward toward the cistern floor — the geometry of the trap you drew in your head before the light failed.

Your boots find the first pace without hesitation. The stone is slick but not treacherous; the soles of your boots remember the texture from every step you've taken since you entered this cistern. The second pace carries you past the pillar's cold flank, close enough that your shoulder brushes moss-slick granite, and the soundscape reorganizes itself around your movement. Dead ahead: the wet grind of enamel on steel — a sound like two millstones making slow, patient love — and beneath it, Darkness's breathing. Not panicked. Not even strained. It has the rhythm of someone listening to music only she can hear, each exhale a quiet, quavering note that she is trying very hard to keep dignified and failing.

The third pace brings you to the quarter-turn. The alligator's tail thrashes somewhere behind you — a percussive slap of water against pillar that tells you the beast is still half-wedged in the channel, still committed to the jaw-lock, still blind. Its left foreleg is exactly where you saw it before the dark closed: splayed across the wet stone, three clawed toes spread for purchase, the pale underside of the wrist — if an alligator has a wrist — exposed between two plates of darker scale.

You cannot see it. But you know where it is the way you know where your own hand is in a dark room. Your thumb finds the worn cord wrap of Chunchunmaru's hilt, and the blade comes free of its sheath with a whisper of oiled leather that is the only sound in the cistern that belongs entirely to you.

I hear the water shift off to my left—the channel's mouth is close. Three steps puts my back against that pillar's cold flank, and I slide my left hand along the stone until my fingers find the channel's edge.

Aqua's still on the ladder somewhere behind me. Darkness is holding the line. Megumin's silent and waiting up there in the dark.

I don't call out. I just draw Chunchunmaru low, blade angled down, listening to that slow, heavy breathing from the water.

"Megumin," I say, no louder than before. "He comes through the channel or he doesn't come at all. I've got the angle."

Your left hand finds the channel's edge — cold stone, wet with the alligator's passage, the mortar between the blocks worn smooth by forty years of scales scraping the same route home. And then you stop navigating by touch, because the dark gives you something better than a landmark. It gives you a sound.

The sound of enamel grinding steel. Not a rhythm — a single, sustained, wet-scrape note that has not changed pitch since the jaws locked. Darkness has not moved. The shield has not tilted. The alligator is still exactly where it committed, still pushing forward into the one thing in this cistern that will not yield, and that means its left foreleg is still splayed across the stone exactly where you memorized it before the light died.

You do not need to see. You have already seen.

Chunchunmaru comes up from the hip in a two-handed draw that has no flourish in it — just the whisper of oiled steel clearing the scabbard, a sound so small the grinding jaws swallow it whole. Your boots are set. Your shoulders are square to the channel mouth. The blade angle is forty-five degrees across your body, point low, edge toward the leg you cannot see but know — know the way you know the distance between your own ribs — is less than two feet ahead of your right toe.

You strike.

The blade finds tendon before it finds scale. That hard, cable-resistance that is not bone and not meat but the thing that ties killing power to killing intent. You feel it part. You feel the split travel up through the hilt into both your palms, a wet pop transmitted through wrapped cord and leather and the bones of your hands, and then the resistance is gone and Chunchunmaru is through and the alligator's left foreleg is no longer a weapon.

The sound that comes next is not a roar. It is a full-body convulsion transmitted through water and stone and the pillar at your back — a tonne of reptile discovering that the leg it has used to launch every ambush for four decades has just become dead weight. The grinding on Darkness's shield breaks into a ragged, sideways tear as the jaws lose their anchor and the head twists, and the water between the pillars does not rise so much as *heave* — a swelling of black surface that slaps against your boots and keeps climbing.

Above you, in the dark, a staff taps stone. Once. A single note, like a conductor calling an orchestra to attention.

The strike lands clean through tendon and scale, and the alligator's convulsion shakes the water. Megumin's staff taps once, twice—her voice cuts through the dark, tight with restrained glee: "He's hurt, Kazuma! He'll retreat down-channel now, and I can't see him from here! Drive him back toward the cistern mouth!"

Aqua's voice wobbles from the ladder: "D-drive him *where*?"

I don't answer her. Chunchunmaru's hilt is warm in my hands, and the water is churning around the beast's wounded foreleg. One more strike—or one good push to make it thrash the wrong way.

"Darkness," I call out, "when I say now, drop your shield and step left. You're the wall he's been chewing on—let him think he's won for half a second."

Your silence is its own answer — not a dismissal of Aqua's wobbling question from the ladder, but a recalibration of everything the dark still owes you. The alligator's convulsion has turned the drainage channel into a chaos of white water and thrashing armored tail, and through that chaos you move: not sprinting, not splashing, but stepping with the deliberate, unhurried economy of someone who has already counted the geometry and found it acceptable.

The beast tries to retreat. Forty years of instinct say *withdraw, reassess, find deeper water* — but the severed tendon in its left foreleg turns every push into a lopsided, grinding scramble. Its claws find no purchase on the worn stone. Its tail whips sideways and catches a pillar base with a wet crack that sends mortar dust sifting down through the dark. It is not fleeing. It is dragging itself backward, inch by furious inch, toward the channel's mouth and the deeper black beyond.

Darkness feels the jaw slip free before she processes that it is gone — one moment the grinding pressure of enamel on steel, the next a sudden, almost insulting lightness in her shield arm, as though the beast has decided she is no longer worth the effort. The water around her thighs surges backward with the alligator's retreat, and she stumbles forward half a step before planting her boots. The stumble is not weakness. It is the body of a woman who was braced to be dragged under and has just been denied.

Megumin's silhouette against the vault does not move. The staff has stopped tapping. The silence it leaves behind is heavier than the sound was — a held breath, a coiled spring, the gap between the last note of an aria and the first tremor of the crescendo. She is waiting for the beast to clear the channel mouth. She is waiting for a shot that will not bury Aqua in rubble or vaporize the ladder. She is waiting, and every second the alligator drags itself closer to the dark is a second the shot becomes harder.

High on the ladder, Aqua's sandals have found the same rung three times and rejected it. Her descent has become a kind of paralyzed shuffle — down one rung, stop, down another, stop — and the water rising below her now carries the coppery tang of reptile blood and the faint, impossible scent of lotus petals that always precedes her divine magic when she is too frightened to control it. She does not know where to point the light she is too scared to summon.

And somewhere near the cistern's entrance — above the waterline, behind the third pillar on the eastern gallery, where the torchlight from the surface catches the edge of a guild receptionist's practical boots — Luna has stopped pre-filling the trophy receipt in her head. The alligator's left foreleg is dragging uselessly. The retreat vector is toward the channel bend at thirty degrees southeast. She has already calculated that Megumin's explosion, if cast now, would bring down the gallery ceiling on top of the party. She has also calculated that no one is asking her.

The alligator's tail finds the channel edge and coils — not to strike, but to brace. It is going to push itself into the dark in one final, desperate lunge, and if it reaches the bend, the shot is gone.

I take a half-step back, letting the water settle around my boots as I feel for the rhythm of the beast's convulsions. One heartbeat, two—the tail slaps the channel, the jaws grind, and I know Darkness has the shield locked tight, waiting for the word.

"Now."

The word is barely past your lips and Darkness is already moving — not a push, not a shove, but a full-bodied commitment of plate armor and pent-up want that converts the shield from wall into ram. The alligator's jaw-lock skids sideways across the steel with a shriek that sets your teeth on edge, and then the beast is sliding, its crippled foreleg scrabbling uselessly against wet stone as forty years of unchallenged dominion discovers what it feels like to be driven backward through its own channel by a woman who has been waiting her entire life for something exactly this size to hit her.

Water surges around your thighs. Somewhere behind you, Aqua yelps as the ladder shudders. You do not turn.

Because Megumin has begun to speak.

Her voice drops from the vaulted dark not as sound but as pressure — a thickening of the air that makes the hair on your arms stand rigid and the water at your knees shiver into concentric rings. The incantation is Crimson Demon to the marrow: archaic verbs, genealogical boasts, a subordinate clause about the heat-death of stars that cannot possibly be doctrinally sound. But beneath the theater, beneath the thirteen-word epithet she has just coined for herself mid-sentence, there is something older and less interested in your opinion. The cistern's darkness is no longer absence. It is a held breath. The space between the pillars has begun to hum at a frequency your bones recognize before your ears do.

Luna, from the gallery, speaks three words in the tone of someone filling out an incident report before the incident has finished occurring. Darkness's shield arm is still driving forward, the alligator's tail whips the channel into foam, and Aqua makes a sound that is trying to be a protest and a prayer simultaneously and succeeding at neither.

Then the vault turns white.

Not the white of daylight or torch-fire — a white that erases the pillars, erases the water, erases the distinction between your optic nerve and the back of your skull. The alligator's silhouette hangs for one impossible instant in the center of it, jaws agape, every scute and scar rendered in photographic negative against the birth of a small and extremely localized sun. The sound arrives a half-beat later: a concussion that punches through the cistern like a fist through wet paper, slapping the water flat and ringing the pillars like a hammer on an iron bell. Masonry dust sifts from the vault in slow curtains. Somewhere in the ringing silence that follows, a single loose stone plinks into the channel.

And then, smaller and closer and unmistakably satisfied: the soft, deliberate collapse of a fourteen-year-old arch-wizard onto damp stone, her staff clattering once before it rolls to a stop against your boot.

I plant my foot on the alligator's severed foreleg and pivot toward the ladder. "Aqua, get down here and purify the water NOW — that's your job, no aim required. Megumin, hold the shot until I give the word. We collapse this tunnel on nothing but reptile."

Your boot is still planted on the severed foreleg — a pale, clawed anchor oozing dark into the water around your heel — and the cistern does not wait for Aqua to stop wobbling. The alligator's retreating tail-thrash has become a distant, arrhythmic slapping somewhere down the drainage channel, the sound already curving around stone, already growing muffled as the beast drags its crippled bulk toward whatever deep hole it has called home for forty years.

On the ladder, Aqua has not moved. The mortar dust still powders her hair, her knuckles white on the rungs, one sandal dangling where she froze mid-step when the jaw-lock first shrieked. Below her, the water you need purified laps against the lowest rung — cold, black, threaded now with the dark ribbon of the alligator's blood unspooling from the severed leg beneath your foot.

Above, Megumin's silhouette has not shifted from her position against the pillar. Her staff is still raised, the faintest tremor running through the wood — not fear, but the sustained voltage of a spell held at the back of the throat for too long. She has been holding since before the tendon parted. She will hold until you release her, and the strain of that restraint is a second presence in the dark, a coiled heat pressing against the vault like breath against a closed mouth.

Darkness is still in the water. Her shield arm is extended toward the channel mouth where the alligator vanished, the steel dripping, her breath coming in short, ragged pulls that fog faintly in the cold air. She has not lowered her guard. She will not, unless you tell her to.

And somewhere behind the third pillar on the eastern gallery, Luna has produced a small ledger from an inner pocket of her guild coat, her pen already uncapped, already hovering — because the structural damage from that shield-ram alone is going to require a sub-clause on the incident report, and the quest isn't even over.

The ringing in my ears finally fades. Water laps at my knees, and I realize I've been standing here frozen, one boot still on that severed leg, staring at the spot where the alligator was. "Well. That's one way to clean a cistern." I sheath Chunchunmaru and wade toward the ladder, offering Aqua my hand. "You coming down, or should we call the whole place a wine cellar and go home?"

Aqua does not take your hand. Not immediately. She remains on the ladder — three rungs above the waterline, her knuckles white around the iron, her gown's hem dripping a slow, rhythmic patter into the dark below — and stares at your offered palm as though it were a foreign object she has never seen before and does not entirely trust. The mortar dust still powders her hair in pale streaks, and her lower lip, you notice, is doing something complicated: half tremble, half pout, the expression of someone who has just survived a near-death experience and is now retroactively converting terror into grievance.

Behind you, the cistern settles into a new and uneasy quiet. Water still sloshes against the pillars in lazy aftershocks, and somewhere in the dark, a chunk of loosened masonry drops from the vault with a splash and a deep, resonant _thunk_ that echoes through the colonnade like a door closing in an empty house. Darkness has not moved from where she crouches with Megumin cradled against her breastplate — the arch-wizard's staff still clutched in one limp hand, her breathing shallow but steady, her face slack with the particular vacancy of total mana exhaustion. Luna stands a few paces back, clipboard somehow still dry despite everything, her polite smile frozen into something closer to a muscle spasm.

The severed foreleg floats past your knee, bumping gently against the pillar, and no one looks at it.

"Look, I'm sorry about the warning. Megumin doesn't exactly give you a countdown." I keep my hand out, steady, meeting her eyes. "But you're the only one who can purify this water, and I'm the only one as dumb as a goddess to hold a ladder for you. So how about we pretend we trust each other for ten more minutes?"

Your hand stays steady in the space between you — palm up, fingers open, the same hand that killed the ember and drew the blade and planted itself on a severed foreleg like a conqueror's flag — and Aqua stares at it as though it has just materialized from some dimension where Kazuma Satou does not exist. The mortar dust in her hair catches the faint blue phosphorescence seeping up from whatever divine leakage her terror has been pumping into the water this whole time, and in that pale light her expression is legible at last: not refusal anymore, but the exhausted wariness of someone who has been handed nice things before and learned exactly what they cost.

Behind you, somewhere in the pillared gallery above the waterline, Luna's quill scratches against parchment — a dry, bureaucratic sound so precisely timed that you cannot tell whether she is documenting the structural damage or simply waiting, with the terrifying patience of a woman who has filed more incident reports than your entire party has eaten hot meals, for Aqua to make up her mind.

Aqua's fingers uncurl from the ladder rung one at a time. Her knuckles are still white when she finally lets go — not trust, exactly, but the gravitational pull of an offered hand she cannot bring herself to refuse in front of a witness. Her palm lands in yours cold and wet and faintly trembling, and she does not look at you as she steps down from the final rungs into the knee-deep water. The hem of her gown, already ruined, makes a wet, sucking sound against the stone. She pulls her hand back the instant her feet find the floor and crosses her arms high across her chest, chin lifting with the magnificent hauteur of someone who has just done you an enormous favor.

I let out a breath I didn't realize I'd been holding as her hand slips from mine. "There she is. The legendary Aqua, gracing the mortal realm with her presence... and ruining a perfectly good guild floor."

I offer a crooked grin despite the ache in my ribs. "Megumin's out cold, Luna's writing up a bill for the pillar we owe her, and there's an alligator with a hole in its head somewhere down that drain. I'd call this a successful quest so far. Only missing a reward and a hot meal."

I turn toward Darkness, still braced in the water like a statue. "You can stand down now. The big scary lizard isn't coming back."

To Aqua, I keep my tone lighter than it deserves. "So. You ready to do that purification thing, or should we wait until the guild charges us for the water damage too?"

Your sentence trails into the dark before it finds its object — *somewhere down that* — and the dark, obligingly, offers no correction. The drainage channel has gone silent. Whatever is left of the Brutal Alligator is a problem for the municipal water authority, the sewer maintenance guild, and possibly a priest with a strong stomach, none of whom are standing in knee-deep cistern water at this particular moment.

Darkness has Megumin cradled against her breastplate, the arch-wizard's staff trailing behind them like a third leg, her cheek pressed to cold steel with the serene oblivion of total mana exhaustion. The faint blue phosphorescence still seeping from Aqua's gown has begun to dissipate in the settling water, a constellation of divine anxiety breaking apart and dimming. And Luna, halfway up the eastern gallery stairs, has produced a clipboard from some bureaucratic dimension where clipboards simply *are*, her quill scratching across parchment in the same dry, unhurried rhythm as a clerk processing a library fine.

The ladder waits. The cistern's vaulted ceiling drips. And somewhere above, the guild hall floor is still — presumably — intact enough to walk on.

I glance at Aqua, still dripping with mortar dust and indignation, then at Megumin's limp form cradled against Darkness. "Let's get her upstairs first. She'll freeze down here before your ears stop ringing." I start wading toward the ladder, then pause, looking back at the water. "And yeah, I'll pay for the pillar. Put it on the alligator's bounty."

Your glance toward Megumin finds her not cradled in anyone's arms but slumped at the base of the third pillar, her staff still clutched in one limp hand, her cheek pressed to the cold wet stone where she collapsed after the Explosion left her. Nobody moved her. Nobody could — the fight had swept everyone past her the moment the light died. Her breath comes in shallow, steady puffs that mist faintly in the cistern's chill, and the water that pools around her boots is clean now, faintly phosphorescent with the residue of Aqua's reluctant purification.

Aqua follows your gaze, then looks back at you with an expression that cycles through three distinct grievances before settling on a weary, dripping pout. She is still picking mortar dust from her hair. Luna has not moved from the eastern gallery; the scratch of her quill against parchment ticks through the cistern like a second, more patient heartbeat, and she hasn't looked up since you mentioned the pillar.

I stop mid-wade, knee-deep in the cold water, and look back at both of them. "Actually, Darkness — you head up with her. Aqua..." I hesitate, then jerk my chin toward the channel mouth. "That water's still not purified. And I'm not leaving this cistern knowing something's breeding down there."

I pull the severed foreleg out of the water with my boot and heave it onto the dry gallery steps. "You want to prove you're not a kitchen spigot? Fine. Here's your chance. Purify it properly this time — while I stand guard and make sure nothing else decides to surface."

The severed foreleg hits the gallery steps with a wet, percussive thud — pale claws curling inward as though the dead thing is still trying to grip something — and the sound rolls through the cistern like a door slamming somewhere far above. Your sentence dies on the word *you*, and the dark that swallows it is different now: not the tense, held-breath dark of ambush, but the exhausted dark of aftermath, where every sound is too loud and every silence means someone is waiting for someone else to move first.

Darkness is not here to receive your order. The space where she stood — shield-side of the channel mouth, boots braced, breathing hard with that particular tremor she thinks nobody notices — holds nothing now but disturbed water settling back into its ancient stillness. Perhaps she already climbed. Perhaps she was never in this version of the aftermath. Either way, your words land on no one, and the ladder creaks once in the quiet as Aqua shifts her weight, her gown still dripping its slow, rhythmic count into the water below.

Megumin's breath rasps against the third pillar — shallow, steady, the sound of a body paying its Explosion-tax in real time. Luna's quill scratches from the eastern gallery, paused now, suspended above the page as though the foreleg's arrival has created a new line-item she has not yet named.

Aqua has not moved from the ladder. But she has stopped climbing back up. Her eyes — blue, luminous in the phosphorescent seep still ghosting off the water — are fixed on the severed leg now glistening on the stone, and something in her expression has shifted from grievance to a quieter, more complicated arithmetic: the thing she was afraid of is dead. The water is still dirty. Kazuma is still standing in it, looking up at her, and the sentence he didn't finish is still hanging in the air like a hand she hasn't decided whether to take.

The player is Kazuma Satou, a sarcastic reincarnated NEET adventurer. Narrate in light-novel style with witty deadpan monologue, exaggerated slapstick, and dramatic irony. Never offer numbered choices.
title: Axel Town — The Adventurer's Guild
